headline: GDPR complaint filed against dict.cc for 1,741 "informed" consents with one click
summary: Privacy organization noyb has filed a complaint, arguing that requiring users to consent to 1,741 partners with a single click makes informed consent impossible, violating GDPR.
details: Privacy organization noyb has filed a complaint against the online dictionary dict.cc. The complaint alleges that dict.cc violates GDPR by nudging users into consenting to online tracking by a staggering 1,741 "partners" with a single click.

GDPR requires consent to be freely given, informed, specific, and unambiguous. This practice makes it impossible for users to truly understand who accesses their data and how it's used, a common issue with sites relying on extensive online advertising.

Online advertising companies track browsing habits, interests, and location for personalized ads. EU privacy law mandates explicit consent for such tracking, leading to the ubiquitous consent banners seen today.

dict.cc's consent request lists 1,741 partners, whose privacy policies would take an estimated 170 hours to read thoroughly. This makes obtaining "informed consent" practically inconceivable, as partners often forward data further.
Felix Mikolasch, a data protection lawyer at noyb, stated it's "ridiculous to assume that this would allow for an informed decision." This widespread issue affects many popular websites.

noyb has filed the complaint with the Austrian Data Protection Authority, arguing dict.cc lacks a valid legal basis for processing data. They request the DPA to order data deletion and inform all recipients of the deletion.

Furthermore, noyb proposes a fine to deter future breaches and suggests a wider ban or referral to the European Data Protection Board. Martin Baumann, another noyb lawyer, emphasized that consenting to thousands of partners is fundamentally wrong.

headline_marked: [[Run AI Models Locally with Ollama]]: Full Privacy, Zero Cost
headline: Run AI Models Locally with Ollama: Full Privacy, Zero Cost
summary: Ollama is an open-source tool that allows users to run powerful LLMs like Llama 3 and Mistral on their own hardware, ensuring data privacy and eliminating API costs.
details: Ollama is an open-source tool designed to run large language models (LLMs) directly on your local machine. This provides full privacy, as data never leaves your hardware, and eliminates API costs associated with cloud-based AI services.
Installation is quick, typically taking only two minutes. Users can deploy popular models such as Llama 3, Mistral, and Gemma, gaining complete control over their AI operations without rate limits.

The platform offers significant cost savings. While cloud services like OpenAI's GPT-4 can cost $0.03 per 1K output tokens, running Llama 3 on Ollama incurs only electricity costs, potentially saving over $10,000 annually for high-volume use.

Ollama ensures compliance with regulations like GDPR and HIPAA by default, making it ideal for sensitive applications in healthcare, legal, and finance. Client documents and patient data remain confidential and secure on-premises.

Developers can also leverage Ollama for tasks like code review without proprietary code leaving their environment. This local execution capability supports internal knowledge bases and confidential enterprise AI initiatives.
